title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 16
paragraphs: So Xerxes spoke to him, and Artabanus was unwilling at first to obey the command, since he did not consider himself worthy to sit on the royal throne; but at last, pressed further, he did as he was bidden, having first spoken these words: “It is equally good, in my judgment, O king, whether a man has wisdom of his own or is willing to follow the counsel of someone who speaks well; and you, who have both of these goods, are being led astray by the communications of bad men. It is as they say of the sea, which of all things is the most useful to men, yet is prevented by the blasts of winds falling upon it from behaving according to its own nature. As for me, it was not that I was so pained by being spoken to harshly by you, as that, when two opinions were laid before the Persians — one tending to increase wanton arrogance, the other tending to check it and to say that it was a bad thing to teach the soul to keep striving for more than it already has — when such opinions were set before us, you chose the one more dangerous both for yourself and for the Persians. And now that you have turned to the better counsel, you tell me that when you were disposed to let go the expedition against the Greeks, a dream came haunting you, sent by some god, forbidding you to abandon the enterprise. But here too, my son, you err: this is not of the Divinity. The dreams of sleep that come wandering to men are, as I — older by many years than you — will tell you, of this nature: the visions of dreams usually hover above us in the shape of the things we were thinking about during the day, and we in the days before had been very much taken up with this campaign. If, after all, this is not what I take it to be but is something divine, you have summed the matter up in what you said. Let it appear, as you say, to me as well, and give its commands. But if it wants to appear to me at all, it is under no more obligation to appear because I am wearing your clothes than it would be if I had my own, nor any more if I sleep in your bed than if I sleep in my own. For whatever this thing is that appears to you in your sleep, surely it is not so foolish as to see me and think that I am you just because the clothing is yours. What we must now find out is this: whether it will ignore me, not thinking fit to appear to me whether I am in my own clothes or in yours, and will continue to haunt you instead. For if it indeed haunts you continually, I too shall be disposed to say that it is of the Divine. But if you have resolved that this is how it must be, and there is no turning your resolve aside, and I must sleep in your bed, then, when I do these things, let it appear to me as well; until then, I shall hold to the opinion I now have.”
